nodes.title: What Is Technology?
nodes.summary: Technology is a means to do something faster, cheaper, stronger, safer, or more effectively; AI belongs in a continuum from the wheel and printing press to modern automation.

nodes.title: AI Is Not the Problem
nodes.summary: AI is not inherently evil; purpose, proportion, sequencing, and downstream consequences matter.

nodes.title: Paradox of Automation
nodes.summary: Individually rational automation can become collectively destructive when labor-income elimination undermines aggregate demand and firms' own markets.

nodes.title: Missing First Rung
nodes.summary: Reduced hiring of entry-level workers can damage the labor pipeline even before mass layoffs appear.

nodes.title: Cognitive vs Physical Automation
nodes.summary: Information jobs are easier to automate first; dexterous, site-specific physical work requires more engineering and generally comes later.

nodes.title: 100-Person Island
nodes.summary: One robot owner replaces 99 workers. Productive capacity explodes while purchasing power disappears.

nodes.title: Valley Before Abundance
nodes.summary: Even if AI eventually creates abundance, the transition may include unemployment, demand collapse, asset stress, unrest, and political instability.

nodes.title: Money, Scarcity & Allocation
nodes.summary: Zero economic profit is not zero price. Scarce goods still require an allocation mechanism.

nodes.title: Nature, Overshoot & Equilibrium
nodes.summary: Nature rebalances overshoot ruthlessly; AI/economic systems may self-correct similarly unless humans design gentler feedback mechanisms.

nodes.title: Ethical AI Transition
nodes.summary: Fairness, speed, warning, support, and sequencing matter. Progress should not ambush people who have no realistic time to adapt.

nodes.title: AI Layoffs & Hiring Evidence
nodes.summary: Track layoffs, reduced hiring, entry-level exposure, occupation changes, and employer disclosures tied to AI.

nodes.title: Autonomous Robotics
nodes.summary: Track controlled-environment robotics first, then less structured physical work.

nodes.title: Automation of Danger vs Livelihood
nodes.summary: Automating danger can protect humans; automating livelihoods changes the income-and-demand system.

nodes.title: Paradox of Thrift Analogy
nodes.summary: What is rational for one actor can be destructive when everyone does it.

nodes.title: Race to Automate / Tragedy of Commons
nodes.summary: Firms may automate because competitors will; no conspiracy is required for collectively destructive outcomes.

nodes.title: Expertise Pipeline Problem
nodes.summary: If junior roles disappear, future senior professionals may never accumulate the experience organizations still need.

nodes.title: Controlled Environments First
nodes.summary: Physical automation can arrive sooner when environments are constrained or redesigned around machines.

nodes.title: Claim on Production
nodes.summary: If labor no longer determines income, what gives humans a legitimate claim on machine-produced goods and services?

nodes.title: Social Instability / Revolution Risk
nodes.summary: Rapid unemployment, inequality, and collapsing expectations can create unrest or revolutionary pressure.

nodes.title: Abundance Is Not Infinite Supply
nodes.summary: Land, energy, materials, desirable locations, time, and unique experiences remain scarce even in high-productivity worlds.

nodes.title: Mouse Plague Analogy
nodes.summary: Population/resource overshoot illustrates brutal self-correction when feedback is ignored.

nodes.title: Speed & Fairness
nodes.summary: AI disruption can blindside ordinary people before they understand what is happening or have time to retrain.

nodes.title: Gold Rush / Tulip Bubble Analogy
nodes.summary: Competitive frenzy and fear of missing extraordinary returns can drive capital and behavior to extremes.

nodes.title: Oil Extraction Race
nodes.summary: Individually rational extraction can create collective oversupply; used as an analogy for automation races.

nodes.title: Luddite / Industrial Transition History
nodes.summary: Mechanization, worker resistance, state suppression, and long transition periods provide a contrast with today's faster AI disruption.

nodes.title: Musk No-Money / Abundance Thesis
nodes.summary: Examine claims that AI makes work optional and money irrelevant; distinguish abundance from scarcity and zero economic profit from zero price.

nodes.title: Fossil Fuel Transition Comparison
nodes.summary: Fossil fuels had decades of warning and still have not fully transitioned; AI gives workers far less runway.

nodes.title: Capitalism Has No Brake Pedal
nodes.summary: Competitive capitalism rewards short-term cost reduction and market capture even when collective adoption may destabilize demand.

nodes.title: Government Capture / Follow the Money
nodes.summary: Lobbying, subsidies, pay-to-play incentives, short-term politics, and weak foresight can obstruct transition planning.

nodes.title: Government Failure / Need for Collective Adoption
nodes.summary: One ethical firm cannot stabilize the economy alone; systemic problems require collective rules or shared mechanisms.

nodes.title: Weak UBI Critique
nodes.summary: Very low UBI levels such as $10k-$12k/year cannot support modern housing, healthcare, education, retirement, and middle-class consumption.

nodes.title: Post-Work Meaning & Identity
nodes.summary: Work provides income, structure, identity, contribution, and purpose; mass displacement can create a meaning crisis.

nodes.title: AI Safety vs Economic Safety
nodes.summary: Traditional AI safety focuses on misuse/alignment; economic destabilization from job destruction deserves comparable attention.

nodes.title: Autonomous Warfare
nodes.summary: AI in warfare and life-and-death decision systems is a distinct nefarious use requiring strong ethical limits.

nodes.title: Lifespan Extension & System Design
nodes.summary: Longer lifespans can stress pension, Social Security, healthcare, and retirement assumptions.

nodes.title: Prevention vs Lifespan Extension
nodes.summary: Preventing early death differs systemically from broadly extending lifespan.

nodes.title: Ethical Use Cases for AI
nodes.summary: Use AI for materials, recycling, climate, dangerous environments, firefighting, nuclear accidents, and pandemic prevention.

nodes.title: Economic Profit Tends Toward Zero
nodes.summary: Competitive markets tend to erode supernormal economic profits; this does not imply zero prices or zero production costs.

nodes.title: Capital-Labor-IP Triangle
nodes.summary: AI may substitute for labor and portions of IP/knowledge, concentrating power in capital owners.

nodes.title: Production Without Consumption
nodes.summary: High productive capacity with insufficient labor income creates goods without enough purchasing power to consume them.

nodes.title: Effective Demand / Production Requires a Buyer
nodes.summary: Production is economically incomplete until a buyer is willing and able to transact. Productive capacity does not guarantee profitable sales when demand or purchasing power is insufficient.

nodes.title: Labor as a Factor of Production
nodes.summary: From a firm's production perspective, human labor is an input. If machines or AI can deliver the same result at lower total cost, the economic case for retaining that labor weakens.

nodes.title: Competitive Pressure Overrides Benevolence
nodes.summary: The automation problem does not require ruthless employers. Even humane firms may be forced to reduce unnecessary labor when competitors achieve structurally lower costs through automation.

nodes.title: Continuum of Automation Outcomes
nodes.summary: Automation outcomes are not binary. The future can range from beneficial complementarity and higher prosperity through partial displacement, structural unemployment, and severe economic disruption.

nodes.title: No Guaranteed Human-Labor Frontier
nodes.summary: Past waves of automation repeatedly moved people into tasks machines could not yet perform. There is no established guarantee that economically valuable human-only tasks must remain sufficiently abundant forever.

nodes.title: Entrepreneurship Does Not Solve Demand
nodes.summary: AI may make it easier for almost anyone to create a business, but producers still need paying customers. Universal entrepreneurship does not by itself solve a shortage or concentration of purchasing power.

nodes.title: Attention as a Scarce Resource
nodes.summary: As AI makes creation and production dramatically easier, human attention may become an even tighter bottleneck. Abundant producers can compete for a finite amount of customer time and attention.

nodes.title: Asset-Valuation Feedback Loop
nodes.summary: Structural labor-income decline could reduce retirement contributions and increase withdrawals, potentially changing persistent investment flows that help support financial-asset valuations.

nodes.title: Market Cap Is Not Realizable Wealth
nodes.summary: Market capitalization is shares outstanding multiplied by the prevailing marginal share price. It is not a pool of cash that all shareholders can simultaneously realize at that price.

nodes.title: Main Street / Wall Street Dual Dependency
nodes.summary: Labor income supports both current consumption on Main Street and savings, pensions, and retirement investment flows on Wall Street. Large labor-income losses can therefore transmit through both systems.

nodes.title: Post-Labor Equilibrium
nodes.summary: Highly automated production could ultimately create broad prosperity, but a stable equilibrium may require redesigning institutions built around the work-to-income-to-consumption relationship.

nodes.title: Automation Success as the Risk
nodes.summary: The paradox may emerge not because automation fails, but because it succeeds exceptionally well at producing goods and services while reducing the need for the labor income that historically funds consumption.

nodes.title: Price Effects / Productivity Counterargument
nodes.summary: Automation can lower prices as well as labor costs. POA must test whether price declines and productivity gains can offset reductions or concentration in labor income rather than assuming lower wages mechanically mean lower consumption.

nodes.title: Complementarity vs Displacement
nodes.summary: AI can complement workers and raise their productivity rather than replace them. The unresolved economy-wide question is whether higher output preserves employment, expands demand, or lets fewer workers perform the same amount of work.

nodes.title: Externalities / Not My Problem
nodes.summary: Actors have weak incentives to voluntarily absorb costs they can shift onto workers, communities, taxpayers, the environment, or future generations. Plastics pollution, greenhouse-gas emissions, and automation displacement differ in mechanism but share the problem that private benefits can be separated from broader social costs.

nodes.title: Proper Government / Collective Governance
nodes.summary: When individually rational private behavior creates significant costs for people outside the decision, a legitimate collective mechanism is needed to make those consequences part of the decision. Proper government does not mean maximum regulation; it means competent rules, incentives, liability, standards, taxation, support, or other institutions proportionate to the systemic problem.

nodes.title: Proportional Regulation
nodes.summary: Regulation can itself become unjust or ineffective when compliance burdens and penalties are disconnected from actual harm, scale, culpability, recurrence, economic benefit, or ability to pay. The same fixed fine can be existential for a small business yet trivial for a giant corporation.

nodes.title: Decision-Maker Consequence Gap
nodes.summary: The farther decision-makers are insulated from the downside of choices whose upside they capture, the greater the opportunity for reckless or socially damaging behavior. This applies to corporate risk-taking, externalities, automation, environmental damage, and other high-impact decisions.

nodes.title: Corporate Entity / Limited Liability and Accountability
nodes.summary: The corporate entity and limited liability enable investment and large-scale productive activity, but they can also separate consequential human decisions from personal financial consequences. The policy question is where useful liability protection should end and meaningful individual accountability should begin.

nodes.title: Asymmetric Upside / Socialized Downside
nodes.summary: Executives or institutions may capture bonuses, profits, prestige, and appreciation when risky decisions succeed while shareholders, employees, creditors, taxpayers, or society absorb much of the catastrophic downside. Too-big-to-fail institutions are a textbook case of this incentive problem.

nodes.title: Compounding Systemic Stresses
nodes.summary: AI displacement would not arrive in a clean economic system. It can interact with existing weaknesses in hiring, housing, healthcare, retirement, public finance, education, debt, and social insurance so that combined effects are larger than any single shock considered in isolation.

nodes.title: Empathy Gap / Distance From Consequences
nodes.summary: People are more willing to accept disruption when they believe someone else will bear it. Distance from job loss, discrimination, poverty, pollution, or other hardship can encourage canned individual-blame explanations and reduce urgency, especially when decision-makers are insulated from the consequences of policy or technology choices.

nodes.title: Individual Attribution vs Systemic Evidence
nodes.summary: AI displacement does not require proving that every individual termination was caused by AI. Economy-wide effects can be identified empirically through hiring, vacancies, wages, occupational employment, productivity, headcount, employer disclosures, and comparisons between more- and less-exposed work.

nodes.title: Labor-Market Friction Amplifier
nodes.summary: AI may make occupational switching more necessary while modern hiring systems make switching unnecessarily difficult. Applicant filters, exact-title requirements, credential screens, and weak recognition of transferable skills can prolong displacement even when workers are capable of moving into adjacent work.

nodes.title: Social Insurance Payroll Dependency
nodes.summary: Systems such as U.S. Social Security depend heavily on taxable payroll from current workers and employers. Persistent AI-driven reductions in employment or taxable labor income could therefore transmit beyond individual households into social-insurance financing, alongside effects on retirement contributions and public revenue.

nodes.title: Policymaker Competence / Expertise Asymmetry
nodes.summary: Elected officials govern extraordinarily complex systems despite few formal knowledge requirements. When policymakers lack enough cross-disciplinary literacy to interrogate sophisticated industry, ideological, or advocacy claims, expertise asymmetry can shift practical policy power toward organized interests that frame the problem, evidence, and proposed solution.

nodes.title: Governing Competence vs Political Skill
nodes.summary: Winning elections, messaging, coalition building, fundraising, negotiation, and maintaining office are political skills; governing complex technological and economic systems requires a different mix of broad literacy, critical reasoning, independent expertise, ethics, intellectual humility, and awareness of consequences.

nodes.summary: Preserve purchasing power when machines replace labor; must be framed as system stabilization rather than a trivial handout.

nodes.title: Managed Transition / Work Reduction
nodes.summary: Use productivity gains to reduce hours rather than abruptly eliminate people.

nodes.title: AI Impact / Systems Consequence Assessment
nodes.summary: Assess labor, demand, retirement, housing, tax-base, and social-stability effects before large-scale deployment.
